DURBAN WATER 2022

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
eThekweni’s Water Woes are not new, and they are far from over – Carte Blanche goes undercover to investigate why this coastal city is just not getting on top of a brewing water crisis.

Unique Selling Point:
- DIFFERENT APPROACH TO WATER STORY
- UNDERCOVER
- GOING TO THE ROOT CAUSE OF THE CHAOS

Summary:
Durban’s Beaches are shocking. They’ve been closed for more than half of the year. Why? Sewage in the water. We’ve done stories about it, the blue flag beaches that are no more, the eColi levels are off the charts. But WHY?!?!?!

We do an undercover investigation, venturing into the city’s different water reservoirs, sewage plants and water treatment plants.


Further information:
IN A NUTSHELL
The city is dealing with aging infrastructure that has been severely damaged in the April Floods combined with a lack of resources and the expected corruption element – eThekweni Municipality is in trouble.

The Beaches have been more closed than open in the last year. The eColi levels are off the charts. The infrastructure is either broken or on the brink of failure.

Speaking to insiders in the Water and Sanitation Department – things are bleak – the get a fraction of the budget needed to do maintenance – one of 16 superintendents I’m speaking to has something like 58 orders outstanding. Been put through but not paid for. He believes it’s an evil brew of lack of funds and corruption.

With the storm damage a lot of the sewage doesn’t make it to the treatment plants – so about 40-60% of sewage get treated in some cases – the rest is going into the roads, rivers and making it to the ocean.

When it comes to pumpstations – those get vandalized all the time. Stripped of electrical components – anything of value. Our undercover shows how easy it is to get access.


PUMP STATION STATUS QUO
North
10 vandalised
6 flood damaged of which 2 are coastal
Sewage backing up into people's houses or streets

Central
4 vandalised
Informal settlements causing damage to get power

South
22 were effected after being submerged or debris in the sumps
18 already repaired
7 getting vandalised on regular basis
calculated vandalism where they destroy what cannot be taken

West
least effected by the storm or vandalism possibly as a result of population demographics
Sand in pumps is a constant challenge with debris related problems only in first week after the storm

DANGEROUS GAME - OFFICIALS TAKEN OUT
So far this year two municipal employees in senior positions were murdered on duty. A third was shot in his office in 2019 – all three were senior officials in the Water and Sanitation division.

The insider we’ll be speaking fears for his life – because he has seen his colleagues pay the price when they don’t tow the line.

He has intricate knowledge of the challenges and true state of failing infrastructure.

WATER TEST DISCREPENCIES
Although eThekweni signboards state that samples are taken every second week, the test dates on display varied widely. Some signs indicated that tests had been done on 30 August. Others had test dates for 28 August or 16 August.

The city responded in other media saying : “As recently announced in an urgent public notice, beaches remain closed due to poor water quality. At this point, both our results and the results you shared with us show that the beaches need to remain closed until such a time that test results indicate that the water quality is acceptable.”

It’s not always clear if all or some beaches are open or closed. City Alerts are contradicting. Talbot Laboratories will explain this part.

Lack of transparency
Earlier this year, we exposed how the city flip-flopped several times on beach closures during the New Year tourist season and reopened beaches when its own lab tests showed high readings at several beaches. Even before the devastation to sewage treatment infrastructure from the floods of April and May, a senior city official also attempted to dismiss visibly stained pulses of dark water pouring out of the Umgeni River mouth as the after-effects of heavy rains and invasive water hyacinth weeds.
The city’s lack of transparency on beach water quality has been further called into question by the recent absence of beach water quality results posted on the city’s website.
Commenting on Sunday, Adopt-a-River founder Janet Simpkins said she found it odd that the city was refusing to release its lab results.
“The public has a right to this information. What are the reasons for not disclosing it?” she asked.

WHAT NOW – CAN THE CITY FIX THIS?
Yes, the city can. But they have the money to do it. Not really.

The eThekwini Municipality needs to spend more than R20-billion within the next 10 years to ensure that its water and wastewater systems can support its increasing population, but it simply does not have the money to do so.

That’s according to eThekwini Deputy Mayor Philani Mavundla, who was addressing the South African Human Rights Commission’s (SAHRC) ongoing hearings into water access in KwaZulu-Natal.
He said the council was using ratepayers’ money, which should be allocated for the maintenance and replacement of existing infrastructure, to instead meet the growing water and wastewater demands of its non-paying residents, particularly those in its expanding informal settlements.
This was “a bit unfair”, he said. “It’s a Catch-22 situation that we find ourselves in.”
eThekwini’s head of Water and Sanitation, Ednick Msweli said that to replace the bulk water infrastructure in eThekwini that had already exceeded its design life would cost about R8.2-billion (although he said this was by now probably closer to R10-billion), and replacing sewerage infrastructure of the same vintage would cost about R4.5-billion. To replace water and sewerage infrastructure that is set to exceed its design life within the next 10 years will cost R4.5-billion for water, and R4.5-billion for sewerage.

Msweli cited a study that found that if infrastructure was to be kept in good condition “so that it doesn’t fail as much as ours fails”, at least 2% of the value of the infrastructure needed to be replaced each year.

Working at 2% annually, he said, it would take eThekwini 50 years to do this. Based on an “old figure”, eThekwini should be spending “about R1.6-billion a year” to maintain its water infrastructure alone.
If that number was updated, it was “more likely to be around R2-billion a year” that needed to be spent. Currently, the city is allocating “about R500-million a year for water infrastructure,” he said.
“But the reality of it is that if you are spending R500-million where you should be spending R2-billion, you lose before you start. That is why our non-revenue [lost] water goes up. Our non-revenue water is [currently] 56%. This is not the norm, it is because of the storm damage that we suffered in the last three months, but even before that it was high, I think at over 40 [percent].”
And there was further bad news. Mavundla said that when areas in the city, particularly rate-paying suburbs, became susceptible to either intermittent services or, in the case of Tongaat, no services at all, it affected the budget.

“Before the floods, the city’s water sales for the month of March in Tongaat were R8.9-million and a further R1.7-million for sanitation services. But after the floods, we could no longer bill that R10.7-million total any more.”

SCRIPT: DURBAN WATER 2022

VO: With its warm tropical climate and golden mile beaches, the coastal city of Durban promises fun in the sun.

ONE SECOND BREATHER…. OF HAPPY DURBAN

**GLTICH TRANSITION TO DARK GLOOMY CLOSED BEACH

VO: But look a little closer, and a very different picture emerges.

LINK: Durban beaches are regularly closed to the public, and the reason is no secret. It's shockingly high levels of E.coli readings. It's an environmental risk and health hazard linked to the sewage.

VO: But to better understand this ecoli crisis, we need to go back in time…..

REWIND SEQUENCE

VO: APRIL 2022…..

UPSOUND RAIN….. STORM VISUALS 2 seconds

Catastrophic storms ripped through Durban… 459 people died…. At least 40 000 were displaced causing billions of rands in infrastructure damage across the eThekwini Municipality.

LINK: I was here five months ago when the storms ravaged parts of KwaZulu-Natal, Natal. Today, we're still dealing with the destruction. Surely people deserve much better.

VO: Water and sanitation infrastructure collapsed in some parts of the city. The result is a raw sewage crisis.

SUSHI: IT brought us like sickness inside us. We can't breathe at times.

VO: Sushi Pillay lives next to the Ohlanga river in the Durban Suburb of Phoenix. This has been her daily reality since April.

SUSHI: You see, when you take a plate of food to eat, that smell is coming right INSIDE THE HOUSE, WE can't leave our doors open.

** AUDIO MIX NOTE - REMOVE MAC’s HMM…HMMM….

VO: And it’s the same at a number of sites all over Durban. Raw Sewage flowing into streams, rivers and eventually the ocean. Months later, eThekwini is living with the consequences.

Marine and Environmental Scientist Micole Martens has been running independent water tests since January this year along a number of Durban’s beaches and rivers.

MICOLE: o if you look at the trends of the results, we were seeing non-compliance before the floods just as much as we are seeing it after the floods as well.

VO 4: The city’s water crisis is not new - it’s been a long time coming.

INSIDER: it was about to happen, if the floods didn't happen in the next year or two. Everything would have come down eventually anyway.

VO: ThE insider is a municipal employee with more than a decade’s experience. He says the city is experiencing a crisis caused by aging infrastructure and poor maintenance.

INSIDER: //A lot of the equipment is very, very old and it has not been renewed or replaced. The equipment is taken out, patched up and put straight back. There is no backup equipment.

VO: For this investigation we ventured into some of the city’s critical infrastructure sites from water reservoirs to pump stations and sewage treatment plants.

Over four days, we went to 27 locations along the KZN Coast from Amazintoti to Queensburg, to Phoenix, Blackburn and Westbrook - secretly capturing clips showing a shocking lack of maintenance, crippled infrastructure and brazen vandalism.

VO: Reservoirs across the city store water for public consumption - we managed to freely walk into three of these facilities - gates open, we were able to lift the lids on water tanks - those that had lids, that is. Pumps were easily accessible, some control rooms didn’t even have locks. And while there were guards at some sites, they weren't always easy to spot.

VISUAL MOMENT
UPSOUND - WHAT ARE YOU GUYS DOING HERE?

VO: At this North Coast pump station, there is a guard, and a fence, well part of it. It’s not operational and raw sewage seeps into the stream.

The sites we visited are not isolated. Close to 40 water reservoirs - vandalised. Of the city’s 247 pump stations - around 70 are overflowing, and another 50 - destroyed by vandals.

INSIDER: They've been vandalized prior to the floods and they just haven't been repaired. One pump station, not working is pollution and it ends up somewhere.

VO: And that 'somewhere', more often than not, is the sea.

LINK: So seeing that and smelling that, it's no surprise that this beach remains closed.

VO: Independent tests showed an eColi Count of more than 24000 at Umhlanga Beach. That’s excessively high, considering an acceptable Count for recreational use is 500 per 100 milliliter sample.

MICOLE: what we have been finding over the last Couple months, as they're more often than not, these counths exceeding that limit. /I1M1

VO: High levels of sewage contamination can also cause fish kills - these clips were taken along the Umgeni river.

1 SECOND BREATHER LEAVING SHOT ON THE DEAD FISH SHOT TO BREAK BEFORE STEVE INTRO

VO: Canoeist, Steven Cohen is from Durbanites against Pollution.

MAC // TO THE naked EYE FROM WHAT I SEE to see this water looks beautiful and SERENE AND you can just jump iN.
STEVE: Yeah, it looks can be deceptive. This water is highly contaminated nearly every single week it;s been exceptionally high readings. /

VO: A recent reading at the Kingfisher Canoe Club showed an eColi Count of a whopping 360 000 - way over the accepted recreational use standard.

STEVE: //It’s now become so chronic that, you know, you enter the water at your own risk. there's just a lot of anecdotal evidence of people getting sick all the time from the poor water quality.

VO: The Ohlanga Pump Station is Near an informal settlement called Blackburn - it’s been out of service since the April Floods.

MARK: JOh, this looks awful!. we’ve got a river of raw sewage running down through here into the Olhanga Estaury onto the Ohlanga Beach.

VO: Dr. Mark Graham is a Water Resource Scientist. eThekwini's water crisis isn't unique. Crumbling infrastructure is an issue across the country.

MARK: It's probably the worst I've seen professionally in working in water for this last 30 odd years.// Clearly, the floods have had an impact, but we should never have got to the state where the sewage infrastructure is in such a poor state that we're actually now reaping those those those ill rewards.

VO: It comes down to inadequate long term maintenance and not taking care of ecological infrastructure.

MARK: That's looking after the river systems, which are where the typically with the sewer lines are running. And the more upstream catchment pressure points, overdevelopment, not looking after those those riparian corridors // That's really causing a lot of the problems.

VO: Regulation and monitoring of the water sector falls on the Department of Water and Sanitation. Ashley Starkey is the KZN Provincial HEad.

MAC: Do you think the city is coping?
ASHLEY: Well, it would appear from from what we see of late that the city would would would really need to to to to take drastic measures to to remedy some of these situations. // they moved from a low vulnerability to a high vulnerability that municipality

VO: It’s up to Starkey’s department to keep the city in line - the first step is to issue non-compliance directives and notices, and hope, that the city comes up with a plan.

ASHLEY: We've issued the city with a number of directives in the in the recent past.
MAC: What can your department then do to hold the city accountable?
ASHLEY:we are able to work with other departments to ensure that further action is taken, environmental affairs have fines and others. And we we are able to, to, to seek court into the exact sector to ensure that they implement the action plans.

ADD IN HALF A SECOND BREATH BEFORE VO STARTS

VO: eThekwini Municipality has plans, but does it have the money?

INSIDER: There is budget, but every year the budget becomes less and less. // the demand is getting greater, //. You can't compete with with wear and tear. You can't compete with vandalism. You can't compete with storms.

VO: Ednick Msweli is eThekwini Municipality’s head of water and sanitation. He concedes, the city is struggling.

EDNICK: At the end of the day, whatever you want to do, you need money because it's just clear the city does not have the money that's required.

VO: Municipalities should be allocating 5-8% of budgets to water and sanitation.

EDNICK: //we are under 5% or less //
MAC: Is it being set aside?
EDNICK: Usually it's close to a billion for water and sanitation, but in the current financial year, we are 900 million. // we should be spending close to 2 billion a year and not for one year. That is forever. If we really want to have an infrastructure that's not going to fail.

VO: It was a perfect storm waiting to happen with aging infrastructure on the brink of collapse, and criminal elements that are just not doing the city any favours.

PAUSE A SECOND

During our investigation we saw a number of inactive pump stations. This one in Westbrook - was vandalised at least a year ago. It’s not working, yet there is still sewage coming into it.

VO: At Sea Cow lake in central Durban, the defunct pump station is right next to an informal settlement - it’s clearly a health hazard.

LINK: This is the handiwork of vandals. They've stripped and taken anything of value. And it's been like this for years, long before the storms earlier this year.

VO: Electrical components, cabling and even pumps - vandalised and stolen, Leaving this pump station inoperable

LINK: And when pump stations don't work, this is the result. Raw sewage flowing into the streets.

VO: Ntwana Mbatha lives opposite the Johanna Road pump station.

MAC: how long has it been like this, the pump station not working?
NTWANA: This pump station I think it’s about 5 years that it hasn’t been working/

VO: But before the city can repair pumps, it needs to spend money on securing these sites.

We showed Msweli our undercover footage.

MAC: // normal citizen walks into a pump station, walks into a sewer, works just like that. Gates are not closed. // It's unacceptable.
EDNICK: I think you raise a valid point./it's a challenge that needs attention. vandalism is killing us

VO: But a lack of resources is also killing eThekwini. According to internal reports during the month of September - only 3 waste water treatment works are operating at full capacity.

These visuals are of the Umbilo Waste Water Treatment Works - parts of it have been destroyed... In Queensburgh - you can see water and sanitation pipes completely taken out in the storms.

EDNICK: The process of RESTORING them is underway. There is a backlog in terms of the replacement of infrastructure. It's something that the city is aware of now and they are prioritizing. I think it sometimes is just competing priorities that make it difficult.

VO: While the municipality is eager to get tourism back on track, some argue the city is getting ahead of itself making decisions based on eColi count samples.

MARK That single grab sample doesn't tell you the big picture. it’s just a single snap shot. they may get an indication that it's reasonably acceptable, but the next day there could be a change in water currents // and the quality changes.

SHOT OF BEACH to BRIDGE BETWEEN EDNICK AND THE LINK FROM UMHLANGA GV

LINK: Closed beaches means no tourism and no tourism means no revenue. And with a city that relies so heavily on tourism, you would think fixing the infrastructure would be a priority.

EDNICK: we need our beaches to to work for the economy of this city. //we opened maybe half of them because we attended to the problems that were that were causing those beaches to be closed.

MAC: //Does it mean all our problems are over in the city of ETHEKWINI?
INSIDER: No, no. There's a lot more maintenance that needs to be done before that happens.

VO: Less than a week after the city’s water tests gave the all clear, the authorities had a change of heart, and a number of beaches were closed again.

STEVE: //It's a very real risk that the city is unable to turn this around. And yeah, the golden mile will be no more. Durban will not be known as a tourism destination anymore

** AUDIO NOTE - add music to the black so that studio knows the black is intentional.

ENDS

ONE SECOND BREATHER…. OF HAPPY DURBAN **GLTICH TRANSITION TO DARK GLOOMY CLOSED BEACH VO: But look a little closer, and a very different picture emerges. LINK: Durban beaches are regularly closed to the public, and the reason is no secret. It's shockingly high levels of E.coli readings. It's an environmental risk and health hazard linked to the sewage. VO: But to better understand this ecoli crisis, we need to go back in time….. REWIND SEQUENCE VO: APRIL 2022….. UPSOUND RAIN….. STORM VISUALS 2 seconds Catastrophic storms ripped through Durban… 459 people died…. At least 40 000 were displaced causing billions of rands in infrastructure damage across the eThekwini Municipality. LINK: I was here five months ago when the storms ravaged parts of KwaZulu-Natal, Natal. Today, we're still dealing with the destruction. Surely people deserve much better. VO: Water and sanitation infrastructure collapsed in some parts of the city. The result is a raw sewage crisis. SUSHI: IT brought us like sickness inside us. We can't breathe at times. VO: Sushi Pillay lives next to the Ohlanga river in the Durban Suburb of Phoenix. This has been her daily reality since April. SUSHI: You see, when you take a plate of food to eat, that smell is coming right INSIDE THE HOUSE, WE can't leave our doors open. ** AUDIO MIX NOTE - REMOVE MAC’s HMM…HMMM…. VO: And it’s the same at a number of sites all over Durban. Raw Sewage flowing into streams, rivers and eventually the ocean. Months later, eThekwini is living with the consequences. Marine and Environmental Scientist Micole Martens has been running independent water tests since January this year along a number of Durban’s beaches and rivers. MICOLE: o if you look at the trends of the results, we were seeing non-compliance before the floods just as much as we are seeing it after the floods as well. VO 4: The city’s water crisis is not new - it’s been a long time coming. INSIDER: it was about to happen, if the floods didn't happen in the next year or two. Everything would have come down eventually anyway. VO: ThE insider is a municipal employee with more than a decade’s experience. He says the city is experiencing a crisis caused by aging infrastructure and poor maintenance. INSIDER: //A lot of the equipment is very, very old and it has not been renewed or replaced. The equipment is taken out, patched up and put straight back. There is no backup equipment. VO: For this investigation we ventured into some of the city’s critical infrastructure sites from water reservoirs to pump stations and sewage treatment plants. Over four days, we went to 27 locations along the KZN Coast from Amazintoti to Queensburg, to Phoenix, Blackburn and Westbrook - secretly capturing clips showing a shocking lack of maintenance, crippled infrastructure and brazen vandalism. VO: Reservoirs across the city store water for public consumption - we managed to freely walk into three of these facilities - gates open, we were able to lift the lids on water tanks - those that had lids, that is. Pumps were easily accessible, some control rooms didn’t even have locks. And while there were guards at some sites, they weren't always easy to spot. VISUAL MOMENT UPSOUND - WHAT ARE YOU GUYS DOING HERE? VO: At this North Coast pump station, there is a guard, and a fence, well part of it. It’s not operational and raw sewage seeps into the stream. The sites we visited are not isolated. Close to 40 water reservoirs - vandalised. Of the city’s 247 pump stations - around 70 are overflowing, and another 50 - destroyed by vandals. INSIDER: They've been vandalized prior to the floods and they just haven't been repaired. One pump station, not working is pollution and it ends up somewhere. MICOLE: what we have been finding over the last Couple months, as they're more often than not, these counths exceeding that limit. /I1M1 VO: High levels of sewage contamination can also cause fish kills - these clips were taken along the Umgeni river. 1 SECOND BREATHER LEAVING SHOT ON THE DEAD FISH SHOT TO BREAK BEFORE STEVE INTRO VO: Canoeist, Steven Cohen is from Durbanites against Pollution. MAC // TO THE naked EYE FROM WHAT I SEE to see this water looks beautiful and SERENE AND you can just jump iN. STEVE: Yeah, it looks can be deceptive. This water is highly contaminated nearly every single week it;s been exceptionally high readings. / VO: A recent reading at the Kingfisher Canoe Club showed an eColi Count of a whopping 360 000 - way over the accepted recreational use standard. STEVE: //It’s now become so chronic that, you know, you enter the water at your own risk. there's just a lot of anecdotal evidence of people getting sick all the time from the poor water quality. VO: The Ohlanga Pump Station is Near an informal settlement called Blackburn - it’s been out of service since the April Floods. MARK: JOh, this looks awful!. we’ve got a river of raw sewage running down through here into the Olhanga Estaury onto the Ohlanga Beach. VO: Dr. Mark Graham is a Water Resource Scientist. eThekwini's water crisis isn't unique. Crumbling infrastructure is an issue across the country. MARK: It's probably the worst I've seen professionally in working in water for this last 30 odd years.// Clearly, the floods have had an impact, but we should never have got to the state where the sewage infrastructure is in such a poor state that we're actually now reaping those those those ill rewards. VO: It comes down to inadequate long term maintenance and not taking care of ecological infrastructure. MARK: That's looking after the river systems, which are where the typically with the sewer lines are running. And the more upstream catchment pressure points, overdevelopment, not looking after those those riparian corridors // That's really causing a lot of the problems. VO: Regulation and monitoring of the water sector falls on the Department of Water and Sanitation. Ashley Starkey is the KZN Provincial HEad. MAC: Do you think the city is coping? ASHLEY: Well, it would appear from from what we see of late that the city would would would really need to to to to take drastic measures to to remedy some of these situations. // they moved from a low vulnerability to a high vulnerability that municipality VO: It’s up to Starkey’s department to keep the city in line - the first step is to issue non-compliance directives and notices, and hope, that the city comes up with a plan. ASHLEY: We've issued the city with a number of directives in the in the recent past. MAC: What can your department then do to hold the city accountable? ASHLEY:we are able to work with other departments to ensure that further action is taken, environmental affairs have fines and others. And we we are able to, to, to seek court into the exact sector to ensure that they implement the action plans. ADD IN HALF A SECOND BREATH BEFORE VO STARTS VO: eThekwini Municipality has plans, but does it have the money? INSIDER: There is budget, but every year the budget becomes less and less. // the demand is getting greater, //. You can't compete with with wear and tear. You can't compete with vandalism. You can't compete with storms. VO: Ednick Msweli is eThekwini Municipality’s head of water and sanitation. He concedes, the city is struggling. EDNICK: At the end of the day, whatever you want to do, you need money because it's just clear the city does not have the money that's required. VO: Municipalities should be allocating 5-8% of budgets to water and sanitation. EDNICK: //we are under 5% or less // MAC: Is it being set aside? EDNICK: Usually it's close to a billion for water and sanitation, but in the current financial year, we are 900 million. // we should be spending close to 2 billion a year and not for one year. That is forever. If we really want to have an infrastructure that's not going to fail. VO: It was a perfect storm waiting to happen with aging infrastructure on the brink of collapse, and criminal elements that are just not doing the city any favours. PAUSE A SECOND During our investigation we saw a number of inactive pump stations. This one in Westbrook - was vandalised at least a year ago. It’s not working, yet there is still sewage coming into it. VO: At Sea Cow lake in central Durban, the defunct pump station is right next to an informal settlement - it’s clearly a health hazard. LINK: This is the handiwork of vandals. They've stripped and taken anything of value. And it's been like this for years, long before the storms earlier this year. VO: Electrical components, cabling and even pumps - vandalised and stolen, Leaving this pump station inoperable LINK: And when pump stations don't work, this is the result. Raw sewage flowing into the streets. VO: Ntwana Mbatha lives opposite the Johanna Road pump station. MAC: how long has it been like this, the pump station not working? NTWANA: This pump station I think it’s about 5 years that it hasn’t been working/ VO: But before the city can repair pumps, it needs to spend money on securing these sites. We showed Msweli our undercover footage. MAC: // normal citizen walks into a pump station, walks into a sewer, works just like that. Gates are not closed. // It's unacceptable. EDNICK: I think you raise a valid point./it's a challenge that needs attention. vandalism is killing us VO: But a lack of resources is also killing eThekwini. According to internal reports during the month of September - only 3 waste water treatment works are operating at full capacity. These visuals are of the Umbilo Waste Water Treatment Works - parts of it have been destroyed... In Queensburgh - you can see water and sanitation pipes completely taken out in the storms. EDNICK: The process of RESTORING them is underway. There is a backlog in terms of the replacement of infrastructure. It's something that the city is aware of now and they are prioritizing. I think it sometimes is just competing priorities that make it difficult. VO: While the municipality is eager to get tourism back on track, some argue the city is getting ahead of itself making decisions based on eColi count samples. MARK That single grab sample doesn't tell you the big picture. it’s just a single snap shot. they may get an indication that it's reasonably acceptable, but the next day there could be a change in water currents // and the quality changes. MAC: //Does it mean all our problems are over in the city of ETHEKWINI? INSIDER: No, no. There's a lot more maintenance that needs to be done before that happens. metadata.Summary: Durban’s Beaches are shocking. They’ve been closed for more than half of the year. Why? Sewage in the water. We’ve done stories about it, the blue flag beaches that are no more, the eColi levels are off the charts. But WHY?!?!?! We do an undercover investigation, venturing into the city’s different water reservoirs, sewage plants and water treatment plants.
metadata.Further information: IN A NUTSHELL The city is dealing with aging infrastructure that has been severely damaged in the April Floods combined with a lack of resources and the expected corruption element – eThekweni Municipality is in trouble. The Beaches have been more closed than open in the last year. The eColi levels are off the charts. The infrastructure is either broken or on the brink of failure. Speaking to insiders in the Water and Sanitation Department – things are bleak – the get a fraction of the budget needed to do maintenance – one of 16 superintendents I’m speaking to has something like 58 orders outstanding. Been put through but not paid for. He believes it’s an evil brew of lack of funds and corruption. With the storm damage a lot of the sewage doesn’t make it to the treatment plants – so about 40-60% of sewage get treated in some cases – the rest is going into the roads, rivers and making it to the ocean. When it comes to pumpstations – those get vandalized all the time. Stripped of electrical components – anything of value. Our undercover shows how easy it is to get access. PUMP STATION STATUS QUO North 10 vandalised 6 flood damaged of which 2 are coastal Sewage backing up into people's houses or streets Central 4 vandalised Informal settlements causing damage to get power South 22 were effected after being submerged or debris in the sumps 18 already repaired 7 getting vandalised on regular basis calculated vandalism where they destroy what cannot be taken West least effected by the storm or vandalism possibly as a result of population demographics Sand in pumps is a constant challenge with debris related problems only in first week after the storm DANGEROUS GAME - OFFICIALS TAKEN OUT So far this year two municipal employees in senior positions were murdered on duty. A third was shot in his office in 2019 – all three were senior officials in the Water and Sanitation division. The insider we’ll be speaking fears for his life – because he has seen his colleagues pay the price when they don’t tow the line. He has intricate knowledge of the challenges and true state of failing infrastructure. WATER TEST DISCREPENCIES Although eThekweni signboards state that samples are taken every second week, the test dates on display varied widely. Some signs indicated that tests had been done on 30 August. Others had test dates for 28 August or 16 August. The city responded in other media saying : “As recently announced in an urgent public notice, beaches remain closed due to poor water quality. At this point, both our results and the results you shared with us show that the beaches need to remain closed until such a time that test results indicate that the water quality is acceptable.” It’s not always clear if all or some beaches are open or closed. City Alerts are contradicting. Talbot Laboratories will explain this part. Lack of transparency Earlier this year, we exposed how the city flip-flopped several times on beach closures during the New Year tourist season and reopened beaches when its own lab tests showed high readings at several beaches. Even before the devastation to sewage treatment infrastructure from the floods of April and May, a senior city official also attempted to dismiss visibly stained pulses of dark water pouring out of the Umgeni River mouth as the after-effects of heavy rains and invasive water hyacinth weeds. The city’s lack of transparency on beach water quality has been further called into question by the recent absence of beach water quality results posted on the city’s website. Commenting on Sunday, Adopt-a-River founder Janet Simpkins said she found it odd that the city was refusing to release its lab results. “The public has a right to this information. What are the reasons for not disclosing it?” she asked. WHAT NOW – CAN THE CITY FIX THIS? Yes, the city can. But they have the money to do it. Not really. The eThekwini Municipality needs to spend more than R20-billion within the next 10 years to ensure that its water and wastewater systems can support its increasing population, but it simply does not have the money to do so. That’s according to eThekwini Deputy Mayor Philani Mavundla, who was addressing the South African Human Rights Commission’s (SAHRC) ongoing hearings into water access in KwaZulu-Natal. He said the council was using ratepayers’ money, which should be allocated for the maintenance and replacement of existing infrastructure, to instead meet the growing water and wastewater demands of its non-paying residents, particularly those in its expanding informal settlements. This was “a bit unfair”, he said. “It’s a Catch-22 situation that we find ourselves in.” eThekwini’s head of Water and Sanitation, Ednick Msweli said that to replace the bulk water infrastructure in eThekwini that had already exceeded its design life would cost about R8.2-billion (although he said this was by now probably closer to R10-billion), and replacing sewerage infrastructure of the same vintage would cost about R4.5-billion. To replace water and sewerage infrastructure that is set to exceed its design life within the next 10 years will cost R4.5-billion for water, and R4.5-billion for sewerage. Msweli cited a study that found that if infrastructure was to be kept in good condition “so that it doesn’t fail as much as ours fails”, at least 2% of the value of the infrastructure needed to be replaced each year. Working at 2% annually, he said, it would take eThekwini 50 years to do this. Based on an “old figure”, eThekwini should be spending “about R1.6-billion a year” to maintain its water infrastructure alone. If that number was updated, it was “more likely to be around R2-billion a year” that needed to be spent. Currently, the city is allocating “about R500-million a year for water infrastructure,” he said. “But the reality of it is that if you are spending R500-million where you should be spending R2-billion, you lose before you start. That is why our non-revenue [lost] water goes up. Our non-revenue water is [currently] 56%. This is not the norm, it is because of the storm damage that we suffered in the last three months, but even before that it was high, I think at over 40 [percent].” And there was further bad news. Mavundla said that when areas in the city, particularly rate-paying suburbs, became susceptible to either intermittent services or, in the case of Tongaat, no services at all, it affected the budget. “Before the floods, the city’s water sales for the month of March in Tongaat were R8.9-million and a further R1.7-million for sanitation services. But after the floods, we could no longer bill that R10.7-million total any more.” INTERVIEWS - INSIDER -MUNICIPAL WORKER - AFFECTED RESIDENTS – open sewage line / surfer - SEA WATER TESTING EXPERT – TALBOT LABORATORIES – MICOLE - MARK GRAHAM – WATER EXPERT – BIGGER PICTURE - UNDERCOVER – UPSOUNDS FROM WARD COUNCILLORS - CONFRONT - ETHEKWINI MUNICIPLAITY - CONFRONT – DEPARTMENT OF WATER AND SANITATION
